title: Meteorology: Severe Weather and Storms
summary: Severe weather is read, not recalled. Work from the instruments outward — a station model, a radar sweep, a sounding — to the storm that produced them, the hazard it carries, and the warning that should follow.
objectives: Decode the observations a forecaster actually works from: station models, METAR, soundings, satellite and radar products.
Diagnose instability and shear from a sounding and a hodograph, and say what storm mode they favour.
Identify storm type from its radar signature and predict the hazard that type produces.
Explain how precipitation forms and which temperature profile yields rain, freezing rain, sleet, snow or hail.
Trace a tropical cyclone or winter storm from formation through track and intensity to the hazards at landfall.
Match a watch or warning to the hazard and the protective action it calls for.

units.title: How We Know What the Sky Is Doing
units.summary: Every severe-weather question begins with an observation someone made: a surface station, a balloon, a satellite or a radar sweep.
objectives: Name the observing systems behind surface, upper-air and space-based data and say what each measures.
Decode a station model and a METAR into temperature, dew point, wind, pressure and sky condition.

lessons.title: Surface Networks, Balloons and Buoys
lessons.objective: Describe what ASOS, mesonets, radiosondes, buoys and aircraft reports each measure, and how often.

lessons.title: Reading a Station Model and a METAR
lessons.objective: Decode temperature, dew point, wind barbs, pressure and the pressure tendency from a station model, and the same fields from a raw METAR.

lessons.title: Visible, Infrared and Water Vapor
lessons.objective: Say what each satellite channel senses and which one answers a given question about a storm.

units.title: Reading Radar
units.summary: Radar is the single most examined skill in this event: reflectivity tells you what is falling, velocity tells you what is turning.
objectives: Distinguish base from composite reflectivity and read base velocity for rotation.
Use correlation coefficient and dual-polarisation products to separate debris and hail from rain.

lessons.title: How Radar Sees a Storm
lessons.objective: Explain how a radar beam produces reflectivity, why the beam rises with range, and how base and composite products differ.

lessons.title: Velocity, Rotation and Storm Relative Motion
lessons.objective: Read inbound and outbound velocity couplets, identify a mesocyclone signature, and explain what storm relative motion adds.

lessons.title: Dual-Pol and the Signatures Worth Naming
lessons.objective: Use correlation coefficient and differential reflectivity to identify a debris ball, hail core and heavy rain, and name the hook echo and bow echo on sight.

units.title: Soundings, Stability and Shear
units.summary: A sounding is the atmosphere's cross-section; whether a storm forms, and what kind, is decided in that profile.
objectives: Locate the LCL, CAPE and CIN on a thermodynamic diagram and say what each predicts.
Read a hodograph for speed and directional shear and connect it to storm mode.

lessons.title: Stüve and Skew-T Diagrams
lessons.objective: Trace a parcel on a thermodynamic diagram, find the LCL and level of free convection, and identify a capping inversion.

lessons.title: CAPE, CIN and What Makes Air Unstable
lessons.objective: Relate lapse rate, CAPE and CIN to whether convection initiates and how strong the updraft can become.

lessons.title: Wind Shear and the Hodograph
lessons.objective: Distinguish speed from directional shear, read a hodograph, and predict single cell, multicell or supercell from shear and CAPE together.

units.title: The Setting a Storm Grows In
units.summary: Storms are not random: air masses, fronts, jet streams and terrain decide where and when severe weather becomes possible.
objectives: Identify air masses and frontal types and the weather each produces.
Explain how jet streams, drylines, atmospheric rivers, water bodies and terrain modify storm formation.

lessons.title: Air Masses, Fronts and Drylines
lessons.objective: Classify air masses, identify cold, warm, stationary and occluded fronts on a surface map, and explain why a dryline focuses convection.

lessons.title: Jet Streams and Large-Scale Circulation
lessons.objective: Relate jet stream position and divergence aloft to surface cyclones and severe weather outbreaks, and describe an atmospheric river.

lessons.title: Oceans, Lakes and Landforms
lessons.objective: Explain how sea surface temperature, ocean heat content, fetch, storm wakes and topography change where storms form and how strong they get.

units.title: Thunderstorms and the Winds They Make
units.summary: From a single pulse cell to a derecho, storm organisation follows from shear — and so does the hazard.
objectives: Order storm types by organisation and lifetime and name the hazard each is known for.
Distinguish a downburst from a tornado by its damage pattern and radar signature.

lessons.title: Single Cell, Multicell, Supercell
lessons.objective: Describe the life cycle of an ordinary cell and explain what shear adds to make a multicell, an MCS and a supercell.

lessons.title: Downbursts, Squall Lines and Derechos
lessons.objective: Distinguish straight-line wind damage from tornado damage, and identify microburst, macroburst, squall line and derecho by signature and scale.

lessons.title: Lightning: Charge, Stroke and Detection
lessons.objective: Explain cloud electrification and charge separation, classify lightning types, and describe how detection networks locate strikes.

units.title: Tornadoes
units.summary: The event's signature hazard: how they form, how they are rated, and what a radar shows before one is on the ground.
objectives: Describe tornadogenesis and the conditions that favour it.
Apply the Fujita and Enhanced Fujita scales as damage scales, not wind measurements.

lessons.title: How a Tornado Forms and Dies
lessons.objective: Trace tornadogenesis from a rotating updraft to a condensation funnel and the rope-out stage, and state where and when tornadoes are most likely.

lessons.title: Fujita, Enhanced Fujita and Reading Damage
lessons.objective: Explain what the F and EF scales actually rate, use damage indicators and degrees of damage, and say why EF replaced F.

units.title: How Precipitation Forms, and What It Does
units.summary: The same cloud yields rain, freezing rain, sleet, snow or hail depending on a temperature profile a few hundred metres thick.
objectives: Explain collision-coalescence, the Bergeron process, riming and aggregation.
Predict precipitation type from a vertical temperature profile, and connect precipitation to flooding and debris flows.

lessons.title: From Droplet to Raindrop
lessons.objective: Contrast warm-rain collision-coalescence with the Bergeron process, and explain riming and aggregation in a mixed-phase cloud.

lessons.title: Rain, Freezing Rain, Sleet, Snow and Hail
lessons.objective: Read a vertical temperature profile to predict precipitation type, and explain hail growth, hailstone layering and size reporting.

lessons.title: Flooding, Debris Flows and Snow Load
lessons.objective: Distinguish flash, stream, river and urban flooding by cause and timescale, and connect rainfall rate to debris flows, snow load and travel hazards.

units.title: Tropical Cyclones and Winter Storms
units.summary: Two seasonal systems with their own vocabulary, their own scales, and hazards that reach far from the centre.
objectives: Describe tropical cyclone structure, stages and the conditions that build or kill one.
Distinguish blizzards, nor'easters, lake-effect snow and ice storms, and their hazards.

lessons.title: Tropical Cyclones: Structure, Stages and Track
lessons.objective: Name the parts of a tropical cyclone, order the stages from disturbance to hurricane, and explain how shear, SST and ENSO steer track and intensity.

lessons.title: Saffir-Simpson and Storm Surge
lessons.objective: Apply the Saffir-Simpson scale and explain why surge, not category, causes most hurricane deaths.

lessons.title: Blizzards, Nor'easters, Lake Effect and Ice
lessons.objective: Define a blizzard by its criteria, explain nor'easter and lake-effect development, and describe ice storm hazards.

units.title: Drought, Warnings and Competition Application
units.summary: Slow hazards, the language of official warnings, and the habits that turn all of this into points on a 50-minute paper.
objectives: Define drought and heat wave types, causes and effects.
Match watch, warning and advisory to hazard and action, and work a data-interpretation station efficiently.

lessons.title: Drought and Heat Waves
lessons.objective: Distinguish meteorological, hydrological and agricultural drought, and explain what causes and sustains a heat wave.

lessons.title: Watches, Warnings and What To Do
lessons.objective: Distinguish a watch from a warning from an advisory, name the issuing office, and give the protective action for each severe hazard.

lessons.title: Working a Data Station Under Time
lessons.objective: Given a radar image, a sounding, a hodograph and a surface map of the same hour, build one consistent diagnosis and defend it.
